I found the passage in the raw transcript of the Diary of a CEO episode. The NASDAQ and IPO story isn't Hormozi's. It's Steven Bartlett's.

**Verdict:** The question's premise is wrong. The host, Steven Bartlett, tells this story about himself on *The Diary of a CEO* (E235, 2023-04-03). Hormozi is the guest; he agrees with it and turns it into his own "fish where the whales are" principle.

**Based on:** the raw transcript (auto-captions with no speaker labels). The speaker is clear from context: the teller says "my company went public on a Stock Exchange in Europe" and talks about "our company which is now called flight story." Those are Bartlett's companies, Social Chain and Flight Story, not Hormozi's.

**Bartlett's story** ([source](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5652s) @ 1:34:12)
- On the road show before the IPO, investment banks told him: "if you move it to the NASDAQ the exact same business would be worth four times more which meant that my net worth would be Forex just by taking the exact same business and moving it to a different Stock Exchange". ("Forex" is the auto-captions mishearing "4x".)
- He took the same idea to his own skills. Instead of helping "a local gym and get paid a th000 bucks," he worked with a company in the run-up to an IPO, because "if you have a good story it can swing your valuation by hundreds of millions" (@ 1:35:17). The first one listed at about $3B.
- The deal: the equity he got "for for the 9 to 12 months work that i' done was worth in the region of 7 to8 million" on IPO day, for what was "basically freelance" work. He says that's why he started Flight Story, which began in the IPO market.

**What Hormozi says in reply** (said it)
- "I thoroughly agree with everything you just said". Then: "the biggest debt all of us pay is ignorance," and "a good fisherman knows where to fish" (@ [1:36:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5818s)).
- His own version of the math (@ [1:38:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=5883s)): a 20% conversion lift for a store doing $1M a year earns you about $20K. The same work for a store doing $100M earns $2M. "100x same work." This ties back to his tweet "solve rich people problems they pay better."
- He brings the NASDAQ example back later as a lesson about leverage from capital. Money comes in tiers: friends and family, then institutional, then public. "the fact that the NASDAQ was Forex … There's just significantly more capital in that market and so it same work more zeros" (@ [1:45:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo&t=6347s)).

**What would change this:** finding another source where Hormozi tells a NASDAQ/IPO story of his own. Nothing like that turned up in a raw search for "NASDAQ"; the only hits were the two in this episode.

That idea isn't Hormozi's. "Travel hedging" is a term from his guest, and the vault has no number of credit cards that Hormozi himself recommends.

**Based on:** something said on his channel, but by the guest. I checked the raw transcript and the vault's notes on this video.

**Where it comes from:** The video is "Building a $12,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 25 Minutes" ([yt-MH-IMJxbUY4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MH-IMJxbUY4&t=33s), 2026-02-28). In it Hormozi consults for Joel McDonald, who founded Just Get Out of Town, a business that coaches people on travel points. Joel describes his own method: "The way we help them is through something we call travel hedging, not travel hacking. We differentiate ourselves there." Hormozi's only part in this exchange is asking the question: "So, what's the difference between hacking and hedging?" (@ 0:33)

**The difference, in Joel's words** (@ 0:33–1:07):
- **Travel hacking:** "basically requires that you churn 10 to 20 credit cards a year, and that's why it has such a bad association."
- **Travel hedging:** "choosing the two or three best cards for your individual spending profile, and learning how to effectively use them."
- Joel says hedging "allows travelers to stretch their vacation budgets three to 10 times farther."

So the "2–3 cards" figure is Joel's. Hormozi doesn't endorse it, and the vault shows no view from him on how many cards anyone should have. The transcript is auto-captions, but the speaker changes make it clear who said what.

**What Hormozi did with it:** He treated it as a sales problem, not as travel advice. Joel named his two biggest problems: about 85% of his advertising runs on Meta, and his niche is distrusted because people link it with travel hacking. Hormozi's advice was:
- Model the ads on viral travel content and customers' own videos ("check out this trip that I just booked for under X").
- Score leads on the two factors Joel said predict a sale: credit-card spend over $5,000 a month and travel spend over $5,000 a year. Leads meeting both criteria get called first (@ 18:35).

Those thresholds also came from Joel, not Hormozi.

The Hormozi vault doesn't answer this. None of its 13 sources mention VAT, sales tax or EU compliance; I searched the wiki and the raw transcripts. Anything below about what he'd do is my guess, built from principles he does state.

**Verdict (a guess):** He'd hand VAT to a tool or a specialist so it never takes your time, and keep your attention on the offer and on selling. He wouldn't try to master tax rules himself.

**Based on:** follows loosely from what he said. He never discusses tax compliance.

**Why he'd likely say it**
- **Pay for tools and help instead of building things yourself.** He says to spend early money on "tools, … implementation help, and then … trial attempts" ([[yt-jfW6gL6hKhk]] @ 11:25, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfW6gL6hKhk&t=685s). He calls these "minor investments that will give you huge leverage on your time" (@ 12:30). Software that handles VAT, or an accountant, fits that.
- **Simplify by cutting things out.** He argues "complexity is typically the child of lazy thinking" and that you should focus on the one core promise ([[yt--JLN1d1ZKUU]] @ 1:43, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-JLN1d1ZKUU&t=103s). Running your own VAT returns for 27 countries is the kind of complexity he'd want gone.
- **Where he's credible:** offers, sales, marketing and scaling. Tax isn't on that list. His only tax mentions are "the tax collector" as a way of getting paid and tax savings as a hard thing to advertise.

**On the mechanics (general knowledge, not Hormozi):** In the EU, VAT on online courses sold to consumers is generally charged at the buyer's country rate. Sellers usually handle it in one of two ways:
- Register for the EU One-Stop Shop (OSS), which lets you file one return covering all EU countries.
- Sell through a "merchant of record" platform. The platform becomes the legal seller and collects and pays the VAT for you.

Course-specific details matter. Live courses can be taxed differently from pre-recorded ones, and EU business buyers are treated differently. Check your setup with an accountant who knows EU VAT.

I searched the Hormozi vault, and it contains nothing about ESOPs. That means the premise is off: as far as this vault shows, Hormozi hasn't said how to structure one. I searched "ESOP", "employee ownership", "sell to employees" and "equity stock employees", in both the wiki and the raw transcripts, and nothing came up.

Below is my best read of what he'd say. It's an inference from his documented principles, not his advice on ESOPs.

**Verdict (my inference):** He'd probably tell you to make sure you get paid as early and as certainly as possible. In an employee buyout, a large part of the price is often paid out of the company's future cash flow. In his framework, that means you've taken on the buyers' risk, so you should demand more cash at closing or a premium for carrying it.

**Based on:** follows from what he said (he never discussed ESOPs specifically)

**Why he'd say it**
- **Get paid first, and no matter what.** "whenever you're trying to get paid, you want to go higher up. You want to get paid no matter what. You want to get paid first." ([yt-rMJIOK_FgJk @ 12:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rMJIOK_FgJk&t=758s)). If your payout depends on how the business does after you leave, you sit low on his six-level pyramid. That's the "when X happens, you pay me" level, not "you pay me first."
- **Prefer revenue-based terms to profit-based ones.** "if you're doing a profit share, it's way better to have a rev share. Why? Because somebody can play around their profit. They can overspend." (same video @ 12:38). If you finance the buyout yourself, he'd want your repayment tied to something the new owners can't easily shrink.
- **Charge for any risk you carry.** Delays and difficulty "are all things that you can choose to take on for a premium" (same video @ 14:15). Waiting years to be paid is that kind of risk, so price it in.
- **He's wary of debt.** He says he skews "very close to the Ramsey side" on debt (from his 2026 HVAC consult, per the vault's profile). An employee buyout that loads the company with debt to pay you out would likely make him uneasy for the business you leave behind.

**What he's done:** He's never done an employee sale, as far as the vault shows. He sold two-thirds of his supplement and licensing companies to a private equity firm, American Pacific Group, for $46.2M, and sold his software company to a strategic buyer in an all-stock deal ([yt-x3e73Qn6NOo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x3e73Qn6NOo)). Selling a majority stake for cash to a well-funded buyer is the opposite of a seller-financed employee buyout.

**What would change his answer:** The sources don't give one.

For how an ESOP actually works (the trust, valuation, tax treatment, loans), you need an ESOP attorney and an independent valuation firm. None of that comes from Hormozi.

**He didn't. In the vault it goes the other way: he told the roofer to go all in on door-knocking.** The vault has one roofing consult, a two-month-old roofing company ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]], https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU). In it Hormozi tells the owner to make door-to-door the main growth engine and build a door-to-door sales team. He never says to stop knocking. "Google" comes up once in the transcript, and that's the owner talking about asking customers for Google reviews. Google Ads never come up.

**Based on:** said it

**Why he said it**
- **Door-knocking was the channel that already worked.** The owner was closing about one sale per 20 doors. Hormozi said that being able to go get money on demand is rare: "that reliability of being able to just basically go get money um is something that a lot of entrepreneurs don't know how to do." ([[yt-o64cI6tebnU]] @ 3:16, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=196s)
- **With little time and money, back the highest return.** "I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now." (@ 3:16)
- **Don't switch to a new channel.** "Now I think that in terms of scale, you should go all in door to door." (@ 9:49, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=589s) Then: "It's what you're good at." and "Like I don't think we need to be cute about this." (@ 10:21)
- **Grow it by hiring reps.** "I think you building out this DDD army is like the clear straight shot." (@ 10:54) "DDD" is the auto-caption's spelling of D2D, door-to-door. He also framed pay as commission per door: "want to go make 10 bucks? Knock that door." (@ 10:54)
- **He said it again in the follow-up:** "the first thing we said was go all in on door to door as primary growth engine." (@ 24:27, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o64cI6tebnU&t=1467s)

**What happened:** At the 90-day follow-up, the owner said revenue had gone from a little under $32K to about $247K. Those are his own numbers, and the transcript doesn't say whether they're monthly or cumulative.

**What would change his answer:** The vault doesn't record him giving a condition. Going by his "highest return" rule, he'd only move the budget if another channel clearly paid back more than door-knocking did. That's my extrapolation, not something he said.

If you heard the Google Ads advice somewhere else, it may be a different video that isn't in the vault. Send me the link and I can add it as a source.
